_note: Fictional sources for teaching: every source cited here, and every quotation from it, is invented. See sources.json.
title: The dropped quote
context: Two history students are writing about the penny post, introduced in Britain in 1840. Both quote the same sentence from the same book.
question: Which version uses the quotation better?

versions.label: Version A
versions.text: The introduction of the penny post in 1840 is often described as a turning point in British communication. Before this, sending a letter was expensive, and the cost was usually paid by the person who received it. {{q:For the first time, a servant in Manchester could write to her mother in Cornwall as often as a merchant could write to his agent}} {{cite:fairbairn2018|page:42}}. The number of letters sent increased greatly in the years that followed. Many families used letters to keep in touch over long distances. The penny post was therefore a very important reform in Victorian Britain.

versions.label: Version B
versions.text: The introduction of the penny post in 1840 is often described as a turning point in British communication, but historians disagree about whose lives it changed. {{cite:fairbairn2018|integral|page:42}} {{v:locates|located}} its significance in how far down the social scale it reached: {{q:For the first time, a servant in Manchester could write to her mother in Cornwall as often as a merchant could write to his agent}}. The comparison is telling, because it measures the reform against business correspondence, which had always been able to absorb high postage. Yet it may overstate the case: a penny was still a meaningful sum for a servant, and many could not write at all. The reform widened access to letter-writing, then, but it did not make it equal.

picks.a: A reasonable instinct — Version A's quotation is vivid, and it's correctly cited. But it's 'dropped' into the paragraph: nothing introduces it, and nothing afterwards says what it shows. The reader is left to work out why it's there.
picks.b: Yes. Version B builds a quote sandwich: it introduces the quotation (who is speaking, and what point they're making), quotes, and then comments on it — and even questions it.

reasons.text: B introduces the quotation and then explains what it shows.
reasons.feedback: Exactly — introduce, quote, comment. The comment is where the writer's own thinking appears.

reasons.text: B questions the source as well as using it.
reasons.feedback: Yes. 'Yet it may overstate the case' shows the writer engaging with Fairbairn rather than simply agreeing. That is often what separates a strong history essay from a competent one.

reasons.text: A's quotation speaks for itself, so it doesn't need a comment.
reasons.feedback: A good quotation can feel as though it speaks for itself, but readers can draw different conclusions from it. The comment tells them which conclusion you are drawing, and why.
The quotations are identical. The difference is in what surrounds them.

followUp.question: In Version B, which sentence is the 'comment' slice of the quote sandwich?

options.text: "The comparison is telling, because it measures the reform against business correspondence…"
options.feedback: Yes. It explains what the quotation shows and why it matters. The sentence after it goes further, by testing the quotation's claim.

options.text: "Fairbairn locates its significance in how far down the social scale it reached"
options.feedback: That's the introduction: it tells the reader who is speaking and what point the quotation will make, before the quotation arrives.

options.text: "The reform widened access to letter-writing, then, but it did not make it equal."
options.feedback: That's the writer's conclusion. It builds on the comment, but it's about the reform rather than about the quotation.

notes.text: In history, quoting is normal when the exact wording matters — a vivid comparison like Fairbairn's, or the words of a primary source. But every quotation still needs a job, and the writer has to say what that job is.
When the author is named in your sentence, APA and MLA put the page number straight after the quotation rather than next to the name.
This convention follows American punctuation: a full stop or comma that ends the sentence goes inside the closing quotation mark — unless a bracketed citation comes between them.
This convention is shown with British punctuation: single quotation marks, and the sentence's full stop outside them.

chefsNote: A quote without a comment is a garnish on an empty plate.
